newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ says may intervene to help support Thai baht.
newsitem.headline: BOJ says may intervene to help support Thai baht.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) may intervene in financial markets to help support the Thai baht if asked to do so by Thailand as part of the Asian currency safety net agreement reached in 1996, a BOJ official said.
"The agreement is there, although it is not a thing we would activate unless we were asked by Thailand," the official told Reuters.

Last year, Japan agreed with the monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand to establish bilateral repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crisis.

Such "repo" pacts give participants instant access to cash -- for use to defend their currencies against excessive volatility -- by virtue of them selling their holdings in U.S. government securities to partners with a promise to buy them back later.
On Wednesday, in the first use of this agreement, the Thai central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht.
Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority were also said to have bought the Thai currency after it fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar, though there was no confirmation.
The BOJ official said: "We have an agreement, and if we want to use it, we certainly will.
"But it's not a question of our making the first move," he added.
He declined to comment on whether preparations for such a move are currently in progress.
Earlier in the day, Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said Thailand will defend its currency against attacks in the market by currency speculators.
"We have support from all our friends," he told reporters at a symposium in Tokyo on Asia's future.
The baht was up by late Tokyo trade, standing near 25.500-25.600 to the dollar.
